author: Our World in Data
body:
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) publishes its yearly Mineral Commodity Summaries, with production and reserves data for a wide range of minerals. We combine it with the World Mineral Statistics of the British Geological Survey (BGS). Together, they cover many of the minerals that batteries, solar panels, and electric cars need, with data up to 2025.

The combined data covers more than 150 countries, with world totals for some minerals going back to 1900 and country data for many from the 1970s. We recently updated hundreds of our charts with the latest release.

This chart tracks lithium mining each year. Global lithium mining reached an estimated 290,000 tonnes in 2025, about 30% more than in 2024 and around 20 times its 2000 level. In 2025, Australia was the biggest producer with an estimated 92,000 tonnes; China and Chile came next.

(This data update was led by Pablo Rosado.)

Explore all of the updated data in our interactive charts: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/minerals

author: Our World in Data
body:
📝 New article on Our World in Data: No matter how you ask, more Americans are negative than positive about AI.

Online, the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence are intensely debated. But the online world is far from representative, and what people report in a survey can shift quite substantially when a question is worded slightly differently or when respondents can choose their answer from different options. So instead of relying on just one survey, this article puts together five recent high-quality surveys of adults in the United States.

The survey’s wording does matter. When a middle answer is offered, many people take it — 37% did in Pew’s recent survey — and a smaller share reports a positive view: in both Pew’s and Gallup’s surveys, only 9% chose it.

Yet the overall result is consistent: every survey finds that more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. In Pew’s survey, 52% say they are “more concerned than excited”, and 9% are “more excited than concerned” — a ratio of more than five to one.

When people have strong feelings, they are mostly negative. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an “extremely bad” thing for society, and just 2% said “extremely good”. People’s worries extend to the most extreme risks: in a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% of Americans said they are somewhat concerned and 38% said they are very concerned that future AI systems could potentially threaten human survival.

Concern about AI is not confined to one party: in Pew’s survey, 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI. There is no question that many find the prospects of AI exciting. But what these surveys show is that for more Americans, the concerns are larger.

Read the article by Max Roser: https://ourworldindata.org/no-matter-how-you-ask-more-americans-are-negative-than-positive-about-ai

author: Our World in Data
body:
Global electricity generation has tripled since 1985 — most of this growth came from Asia.

In 1985, the world generated around 10,000 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity. In 2024, it produced just over 30,000 TWh — three times as much.

Three-quarters of this increase came from Asia. The chart shows how generation has grown, both globally and in each region.

Yes, population growth explains some of this. But two other drivers were even stronger: more people gained access to electricity, and they consumed more of it. In the early 1990s, fewer than half of South Asians had access to basic electricity. Today, access is almost universal.

At the same time, electricity generation per person increased by almost 450% — far faster than in any other region. Outside of Asia, it has barely changed. This is why, globally, per-person consumption has only doubled.

This growth has given households more and better energy services, and it has also powered a huge expansion of industry.

(written by Hannah Ritchie)

Explore how electricity generation and sources have changed across the world: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/electricity-mix

author: Our World in Data
body:
The large, sudden decline of life expectancy in 1918 shows how abrupt and damning negative health events can be. It was caused by an unusually deadly influenza pandemic that became known as the “Spanish flu”. This influenza outbreak wasn’t restricted to Spain, and it didn’t even originate there: the earliest recorded outbreak was in Kansas in the United States. But the pandemic was named after Spain because Spain was neutral in the First World War, which meant it was free to report on the severity of the pandemic. The virus spread rapidly and eventually reached all parts of the world.

The range of published estimates for the Spanish flu’s global death toll is particularly wide. A widely cited 2002 study by researchers Johnson and Mueller arrives at a very high estimate of at least 50 million global deaths, but the authors suggest that this could be an underestimation and that the true death toll was as high as 100 million. A more recent 2018 study by researchers Spreeuwenberg and colleagues concluded that earlier estimates have been too high. Their own estimate is 17.4 million deaths.

Estimates suggest that the world population in 1918 was 1.8 billion. So even the low estimate of 17.4 million deaths implies that the Spanish flu killed almost 1% of the world population. In recent years, the flu was responsible for around 400,000 deaths per year — 0.005% of the world population.

Influenza pandemics are not rare, but the Spanish flu of 1918 was by far the most devastating influenza pandemic in recorded history.

Read our article: https://ourworldindata.org/spanish-flu-largest-influenza-pandemic-in-history

author: Our World in Data
body:
Differences in GDP per capita across sub-Saharan Africa are large.

Sub-Saharan Africa is the world’s poorest region. Its GDP per person is around $5,000 a year — less than a quarter of the global average of around $22,000.

But looking at the region as a whole can make it easy to forget just how different the economies within it are. That’s what this chart shows, by ranking GDP per capita across sub-Saharan African countries.

These differences are large. At the top of the chart, Gabon has a GDP per capita of about $19,000, roughly 18 times that of Burundi at the bottom. The gap between the richest and poorest countries in sub-Saharan Africa is even larger than the gap between the region and the world as a whole.

(written by Esteban Ortiz-Ospina)

Read more about what GDP is and why it matters: https://ourworldindata.org/what-is-economic-growth

author: Aziz Sunderji
body:
Much has been written about the K-shaped economy: wealthier households pulling away from everyone else. Less noticed is how sharply this shows up in home prices within cities, along lines of income, race, schools and crime. My new map story, Pulling Apart, follows it through five cities.

In Philadelphia, prices are rising in the rich suburbs. Haddonfield, where the median household earns $151,000, is up 6.8% over the past year. By contrast, they are falling in poorer places: just across the river, in Camden, where it earns only $37,000, they are down 7.8%.

In Detroit, the split follows race. Prices are rising in mostly white suburbs: Commerce Township, under 3% Black, is up 2.7%. By contrast, they are falling in mostly Black neighborhoods: an east-side ZIP code that is 90% Black is down 12%.

In Phoenix, the divide is education. Where most adults have a bachelor's degree, prices are rising: in Paradise Valley, where 72% do, they are up 12%. Where few do, prices are falling: in West Phoenix, where only 8% do, they are down 3.2%.

In Atlanta, I ranked neighborhoods with my "fanciness" index. Prices are rising in the fanciest places: Buckhead, in the 96th percentile nationally, is up 7.6%. They are falling in the least fancy: Forest Park, in just the 6th percentile, is down 5.8%.

In Indianapolis, prices are rising in suburbs with good schools and little crime: in Carmel, students test 3.2 grade levels above average, and values are up 5.1%. They are falling in the city: the near east side tests 2.3 grade levels below, has 80 times the violent crime, and is down 4%.

I made every map here with ProMap, which you can use to explore any neighborhood in the country. The full story takes about five minutes: https://thepromap.com/story/r3c5q7

author: Aziz Sunderji
body:
How are Americans doing, financially speaking? 

My new map story, Pulling Apart, starts with that question. To go by national statistics, Americans are doing just fine: unemployment is low and stock market wealth is booming. But these figures hide how many households are struggling. Wages at the bottom have barely grown, and the poorer half of American households holds just 2% of the nation’s wealth.

It’s the same in housing. National prices have been rising slowly and steadily. But there is no single national housing market. There are, in effect, two worlds within it. In richer, whiter neighborhoods with low crime and good schools, prices are rising and homes are selling. In neighborhoods that are mostly Black and Hispanic, with more modest homes, more crime and weaker schools, prices are falling and far fewer homes sell.

The story maps those two worlds pulling apart across five cities: Philadelphia, Detroit, Phoenix, Atlanta and Indianapolis. Every map in the story was made with ProMap, which you can use to explore the same data for any neighborhood in the country.

Read Pulling Apart: https://homeeconomics.us/promap?story=r3c5q7
